findings.title: Secret in a client-visible flag value: payment_config
findings.subject: payment_config

explanation.title: Payment secret exposed in a public feature flag
explanation.what_happened: Anyone holding the client key, which ships inside the app, can request the production flag list and read the payment_config flag. It contains what looks like a live payment provider API secret.
explanation.why_it_matters: Client keys are not private. A secret stored in a flag value is effectively published to every user and anyone inspecting the app.
explanation.business_impact: Attackers could use the key to act as your payment account, causing fraud, financial loss, customer data exposure, and emergency credential rotation.
explanation.fix_summary: Remove the secret from the flag, store it in server-side secret storage, and rotate the exposed key immediately.

evidence.note: secret detected in value at $.api_secret (acme_live_key)

findings.title: Forging role=admin unlocks admin_panel (segment "admins")
findings.subject: admins

explanation.title: Anyone can switch on the admin panel by claiming to be an admin
explanation.what_happened: In Production, the app trusts a self-reported 'role' value sent by the client. Testing with an outside-style request claiming role=admin turned the 'admin_panel' flag from off to on. No password or special access was needed.
explanation.why_it_matters: The admin panel is a security control, but its gate relies on information the user supplies themselves, so it can be faked.
explanation.business_impact: Unauthorized people could see or reach admin features, risking data exposure, unwanted changes, and compliance or customer-trust damage.
explanation.fix_summary: Stop deciding admin access from client-supplied values. Determine roles on the server from authenticated identity, and enforce admin permissions there rather than relying on a feature flag.

explanation.title: Payment settings flag is sent to client apps
explanation.what_happened: The production flag "payment_config" is marked secret, but its "Server-side only" setting is off. This means client SDKs, such as those in browsers or mobile apps, receive it.
explanation.why_it_matters: Anyone who can run or inspect a client app may be able to read this flag's value. Secret configuration is meant to stay on your servers.
explanation.business_impact: Payment-related settings could be exposed to outsiders, which may aid fraud, expose partner details, or create compliance concerns. The evidence does not show what the flag contains or that anyone has accessed it.
explanation.fix_summary: Turn on "Server-side only" for payment_config in Production. Then review what the flag holds and rotate any sensitive values if needed.

evidence.note: Feature "payment_config" is classified SECRET but the dashboard setting "Server-side only" is off, so client SDKs receive it.

findings.title: Traits of ce***@acmeshop.dev are readable by anyone with the public client key
findings.subject: ce***@acmeshop.dev

explanation.title: Customer profile data readable with a public key
explanation.what_happened: Anyone holding the public client key, which ships inside the app, can look up a customer by email and get back the 3 traits stored on their profile. The test confirmed the traits are returned; their contents were not read.
explanation.why_it_matters: The "Hide sensitive data" setting is off in Production, so personal information is served to anyone who asks.
explanation.business_impact: Customer personal data could be harvested, creating privacy-law exposure, breach notification duties, and loss of customer trust.
explanation.fix_summary: Turn on "Hide sensitive data" for the Production environment and keep personal details out of traits that the client key can read.

evidence.note: Identity stores 3 trait(s); "Hide sensitive data" is off, so GET identities/?identifier= returns them. Trait values are not read by Gatecrasher.

findings.title: Traits of qa***@acmeshop.dev are readable by anyone with the public client key
findings.subject: qa***@acmeshop.dev

explanation.title: User profile data readable with a public key
explanation.what_happened: Anyone holding the public client key, which ships inside the app, can request a user's stored traits from the production identities endpoint. The test confirmed it for one account and returned one trait. Values were masked in our evidence.
explanation.why_it_matters: The public key is meant for fetching flags, not reading personal data. Anyone can extract it and look up users.
explanation.business_impact: Customer personal information could be exposed, risking privacy-law violations, regulatory scrutiny, and loss of customer trust.
explanation.fix_summary: Stop returning identity traits to public client keys, or require a server-side secret. Remove personal data from traits and rotate keys.

explanation.title: Anyone can unlock the premium export by claiming to be a gold customer
explanation.what_happened: Using only the public client key, an outsider sent a request saying their plan was "gold". The system accepted it and switched the premium_export feature from off to on. No login or payment was needed.
explanation.why_it_matters: The feature's access depends on a customer-supplied detail that anyone can fake, so the paywall isn't actually enforced.
explanation.business_impact: People can use a paid feature for free, which means lost subscription revenue and less reason to upgrade to gold.
explanation.fix_summary: Decide access on the server using trusted billing data, not traits sent by the client. Or sign the identity so claimed plans can't be forged.

explanation.title: Internal admin address exposed to all website visitors
explanation.what_happened: Anyone holding the public client key can request the flag list and see a setting named internal_api_url. It reveals a private network address pointing to an admin endpoint.
explanation.why_it_matters: The address shows how your internal systems are laid out. Attackers can use it to aim follow-up attacks at the admin interface.
explanation.business_impact: This raises the odds of a deeper breach of internal systems, with possible downtime, data exposure, and customer trust damage.
explanation.fix_summary: Remove internal_api_url from flags served to browsers and keep it in server-side configuration. Then check that no other flags hold internal addresses.

findings.title: Re-rolling the identifier unlocks early_access_ai (≈9% rollout, ~11 tries)
findings.subject: early_access_ai

explanation.title: Unreleased AI feature can be unlocked by guessing identifiers
explanation.what_happened: The early_access_ai feature is meant for a 10% test group. Anyone can send a made-up user identifier to the public API and see whether the feature turns on. About 1 in 11 tries succeeds, so an outsider can quickly find an identifier that unlocks it.
explanation.why_it_matters: The group is chosen by an identifier the caller controls, so the rollout limit does not protect the feature.
explanation.business_impact: People outside the test group can use or see an unreleased product, which undermines controlled rollout and early-access promises.
explanation.fix_summary: Choose rollout membership using a server-verified user identity, not a client-supplied identifier. Keep truly restricted features off the client-facing API.

findings.title: Production: "Allow client SDKs to set user traits" is ON
findings.subject: allow_client_traits

explanation.title: Production lets users set their own traits
explanation.what_happened: In Production, the setting that lets client SDKs set user traits is on. Anyone with the public client key can assign themselves any traits they like.
explanation.why_it_matters: Any segment that decides access based on a trait can be faked. Outsiders could place themselves in groups meant for staff, beta testers, or paying customers.
explanation.business_impact: People could unlock unreleased or paid features without authorization, which risks lost revenue and early exposure of unfinished work. The evidence shows the setting is on, not that anyone has abused it.
explanation.fix_summary: Turn off "Allow client SDKs to set user traits" for every environment that uses segments for access control. Set traits from your trusted server instead.

evidence.note: Environment "Production": dashboard setting "Allow client SDKs to set user traits" is ON (allow_client_traits). Anyone holding the public client key can set their own traits, so any segment keyed on a trait can be forged. Turn this setting off for every environment that uses segments for access control.

explanation.title: Production feature flag data is not hidden
explanation.what_happened: The "Hide sensitive data" setting is turned off in the Production environment. This means sensitive values tied to feature flags are not masked in that environment's dashboard.
explanation.why_it_matters: Anyone who can view the Production dashboard can see data that should be concealed. The evidence shows only the setting is off; it does not show that anyone has actually seen or misused data.
explanation.business_impact: Sensitive information could be exposed to people who do not need it, raising the risk of accidental leaks and creating compliance or customer-trust concerns.
explanation.fix_summary: Turn on "Hide sensitive data" for the Production environment in the dashboard settings.

evidence.note: Environment "Production": dashboard setting "Hide sensitive data" is OFF (hide_sensitive_data). Sensitive data is not hidden in this environment. Turn this setting on.

findings.title: Unreleased product leaked through flag: early_access_ai
findings.subject: early_access_ai

explanation.title: Flag name reveals an unreleased AI feature
explanation.what_happened: Anyone holding the public client key can list your feature flags in Production. The flag named "early_access_ai" appears in the list, even though its value is empty.
explanation.why_it_matters: The flag's name alone suggests an early-access AI product that has not been announced. The evidence shows the name is exposed, not that the feature itself is accessible.
explanation.business_impact: Competitors or the press could learn about your AI plans early, weakening launch timing, messaging, and competitive advantage.
explanation.fix_summary: Rename the flag to something neutral, and stop returning flags that clients don't need. Serve only the flags each client actually requires.

evidence.note: Name reveals an early-access AI feature that is likely unreleased.
